title: Friendship with the World and Humility Before God
summary: James traces the quarrels among his readers to disordered desires that war within them, and he calls friendship with the world hostility toward God. Since God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble, he summons the double-minded to submit to God, resist the devil, draw near, and grieve over their sin. He then forbids slander and judging, and rebukes those who plan their business as if tomorrow were theirs to command.
story: Chapter 3 ended with a portrait of the wisdom from above, peaceable and full of good fruit, and a warning that jealousy and selfish ambition produce disorder. Chapter 4 shows that disorder at work: conflicts, quarrels, envy, and prayers poisoned by selfish motives. James answers not with a technique for resolving conflict but with a call to repentance, one of the most intense in the New Testament, echoing the prophets of Israel. The chapter then widens to two other forms of pride, speaking against a brother and boasting about tomorrow, and prepares for the fierce words to the rich at the start of chapter 5.
historical:
James's words “you kill and covet” (verse 2) have puzzled readers. Some take them literally, noting that Judea in the decades before the revolt against Rome in AD 66 was marked by violence, including assassinations carried out by radical factions, and that believers could be drawn into such passions. Others read them as hyperbole in the manner of Jesus, who taught that anger toward a brother is akin to murder (Matthew 5:21-22), or take the Greek to describe envy so fierce that it wishes a rival dead. The text does not settle the question.

The merchants of verses 13-17 reflect the mobile commercial economy of the Roman Empire. Roads and sea routes made it possible for traders to move from city to city, set up business for a season, and move on. Jewish merchants were part of this network across the Mediterranean. James's objection is not to trade itself but to planning that leaves God out entirely, an attitude he calls arrogant boasting.
cultural:
Friendship in the Greco-Roman world meant more than affection. Friends shared values, loyalties, and enemies, and to become someone's friend was to take their side. To be a friend of the world, in James's sense, is to adopt the value system of a society organized around status, possession, and self-promotion. His address “You adulteresses” draws on a long prophetic tradition in which Israel's unfaithfulness to God is pictured as a wife's unfaithfulness to her husband (Hosea 1-3; Jeremiah 3; Ezekiel 16). The feminine form fits that image: the whole covenant people is God's bride.

The call to grieve, mourn, weep, and turn laughter into mourning uses the language of public repentance known from the prophets (Joel 2:12-13), when fasting, weeping, and mourning expressed sorrow for sin before God. The phrase “If the Lord is willing” became a common Christian expression, sometimes abbreviated in later centuries, and Paul uses similar words about his own travel plans (1 Corinthians 4:19).
literary: The chapter opens with a question and answer (verses 1-3) that diagnose the source of conflict, then moves into a blast of prophetic rebuke (verses 4-6). The heart of the chapter is a series of ten sharp commands in verses 7-10 (submit, resist, draw near, cleanse, purify, grieve, mourn, weep, turn, humble yourselves), framed by the promise that God gives grace to the humble and will exalt those who humble themselves. The quotation of Proverbs 3:34 in verse 6 anchors the section. Verses 11-12 and 13-17 are two short units, each introduced with direct address, the second with “Come now”, a phrase James repeats in 5:1. The chapter ends with a proverb-like statement that sin includes failing to do the good one knows, a fitting summary of the letter's concern with doing.

outline.t: The source of quarrels: warring desires
Friendship with the world and God's greater grace
A call to submit, repent, and draw near

doctrines.note: James roots conflict in desire, the passions at war within, rather than in circumstances. He also defines sin broadly: “Anyone, then, who knows the right thing to do, yet fails to do it, is guilty of sin.” Omission is as real as commission.

Verses 7-10 are among the Bible's clearest calls to repentance: submission to God, resistance to the devil, cleansing, grief over sin, and humility. The promise attached is that God “will draw near to you” and “will exalt you.”
Friendship with the world is spiritual adultery, a divided loyalty that treats God as one allegiance among others. The double-minded person wants both, and James says that is impossible.
Human life is a mist, and every plan depends on the will of God: “If the Lord is willing, we will live and do this or that.” This is not fatalism but humble dependence on God's sovereign care.

words.note: Hēdonē, pleasure (the root of the English hedonism). James says quarrels come from pleasures at war within, and prayers fail because people ask in order to spend on their pleasures. The word names desire that has become a ruling power, demanding satisfaction whatever the cost to others.

Philia, friendship. This is its only appearance in the New Testament. In the ancient world friendship implied shared values and loyalty, so friendship with the world means siding with a way of life opposed to God, and that makes one God's enemy.

Tapeinoō, to humble or make low. Verse 10 commands believers to humble themselves before the Lord, and verse 6 promises grace to the humble (tapeinois). The pattern of humbling and exalting runs through the teaching of Jesus (Luke 14:11) and returns in 1 Peter 5:6.

Atmis, mist, vapor, or steam. James uses it for human life, which appears for a little while and vanishes. The image recalls the Hebrew hevel, breath or vapor, of Ecclesiastes, and it exposes the arrogance of treating the future as a possession.

christ: Although Christ is not named in this chapter, its pattern is his. Jesus taught that whoever exalts himself will be humbled and whoever humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14:11), and the New Testament presents his own life as the supreme example: he humbled himself to death on a cross and God highly exalted him (Philippians 2:8-9). The call to resist the devil recalls Jesus resisting temptation in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1-11). The warning against judging a brother echoes the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 7:1-5), and the reminder that there is “only one Lawgiver and Judge” points to the God whom the New Testament also presents as judging through Christ (Acts 17:31). The “more grace” God gives to the humble is, in the whole New Testament, the grace that comes through Jesus.

hard.q: What does verse 5 mean, and which Scripture is James quoting?
hard.a: Verse 5 is one of the hardest in the letter. The words are not an exact quotation of any Old Testament passage, so James may be summarizing a scriptural theme rather than citing a single verse, or quoting a writing now lost. The Greek can also be read in two main ways. On one reading, God is the subject: he jealously longs for the spirit (or Spirit) he made to dwell in us. This fits the Old Testament description of God as a jealous God who will not share his people's love with idols (Exodus 20:5; 34:14), and it follows naturally from the charge of spiritual adultery in verse 4. On the other reading, the human spirit is the subject: the spirit God placed in human beings tends toward envy, which would fit the diagnosis of envy in verses 1-3. Translations differ accordingly. The BSB capitalizes Spirit and makes the Spirit the one who yearns, a variation of the first reading in which God's own Spirit longs jealously for his people. Either way, verse 6 gives the answer: God “gives us more grace”, enough to overcome both the pull of envy and the divided heart.

questions: James traces conflict to desires within rather than to other people. Think of a recent conflict: what desire of yours was at war?
What does friendship with the world look like in your setting? Where are you tempted to be double-minded?
How would it change your plans for this week to say sincerely, “If the Lord is willing”?
